passage: Wednesday. Diary, today was good! In art period I noticed Himani drawing a cricket player with a huge bat. I never talk first, but I thought: what do I really know? I know cricket. So I leaned over and said, "Is that a batsman? I love cricket! Who's your favourite?" She looked up, surprised, and said, "Everyone in blue!" We talked about the last match until the teacher told us to stop. Then Himani said, "Sit with us at lunch tomorrow." I felt my chest go warm. It was so easy when I started from something I already liked. I'm going to bring my own bat on Friday. Ojas.

qa.a: Himani was drawing a cricket player with a huge bat.

qa.q: What did Ojas think before speaking to Himani?
qa.a: Ojas thought about a known strength, cricket, and felt brave enough to start talking about it.

qa.a: Ojas could ask what the classmate enjoys doing and listen for a shared interest. Curiosity about the other person gives a starting point too.

qa.a: Himani looked up surprised and then invited Ojas to lunch, so Himani probably felt pleased that someone noticed the drawing and shared the interest.

subtype: Approach: using a shared interest to start talking [Thinking]
passage: On his third day at the school in Sangli, Tejas noticed that the girl in front of him, Sarita, was drawing in the back of her maths notebook. Not flowers. Cricketers. A batter mid-shot, a bowler with one arm high. Tejas had watched every match of the town tournament with his uncle. He thought, "She knows cricket. That's something I can talk about without messing up." At the break he leaned forward. "That's a cover drive, right? The front foot is perfect." Sarita turned around, surprised. "You play?" "Only in the lane. But I watch everything." By the end of lunch they were arguing happily about the best bowler in the district.

qa.q: What was the batter in Sarita's drawing doing?
qa.a: The batter was mid-shot, playing what Tejas called a cover drive.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when he saw the cricket drawings?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and relieved, because cricket was something he could talk about without worrying about getting it wrong.

qa.q: What else could Tejas use if Sarita had not liked talking about her drawings?
qa.a: He could invite her and others to a lane cricket game, since doing something together can start a friendship too.

qa.q: How does Tejas's comment look to Sarita?
qa.a: Sarita is surprised and pleased that someone noticed the details of her drawing, which makes her want to talk.

grounding: It shows a new boy noticing a classmate's cricket drawings and using the shared interest to start talking and make a friend.

passage: Mateo's family had moved to Melbourne from Buenos Aires, and in his first week at school he felt like a spare shoe. On Wednesday, in art, he saw Paulo at the next table drawing cricket players in pencil, with a wicket keeper crouched low. Mateo had never played, but his neighbour had been teaching him in the backyard all summer, and he'd fallen for it. He thought, "This is my chance. I know what a wicket keeper does." He pointed. "His gloves look real." Paulo grinned. "You like cricket?" "I'm learning. I love it." "Lunch. Back oval. Bring your hands." At lunch Paulo tossed him a tennis ball and the new-boy feeling was gone for an hour.

qa.q: Where did Paulo tell Mateo to go at lunch?
qa.a: Paulo told him to go to the back oval.

qa.q: How was Mateo feeling in his first week at the new school?
qa.a: He felt out of place, like a spare shoe, a little lonely and awkward.

qa.q: What else could help Mateo keep this friendship going?
qa.a: He could ask Paulo to teach him a bowling tip, because asking for help keeps a shared interest growing.

qa.q: How might Mateo's comment feel to Paulo?
qa.a: Paulo likes hearing his drawing looks real, and is pleased to find another cricket fan to play with.

grounding: It shows a new boy using a shared love of cricket, spotted in a classmate's drawings, to begin talking and start a friendship.
